content: Clindamycin hydrochloride vaginal ovules are an antibiotic medication specifically approved by the FDA for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis in non-pregnant women. The recommended dosage is one vaginal ovule, containing clindamycin phosphate equivalent to 100 mg of clindamycin, inserted intravaginally once daily at bedtime for three consecutive days. This treatment is not adequately studied in pregnant women, and its use during the first trimester should only occur if the benefits outweigh the risks. Bacterial vaginosis is typically diagnosed based on clinical findings, including a homogeneous vaginal discharge with a pH greater than 4.5, a fishy amine odor when mixed with a 10% potassium hydroxide solution, and the presence of clue cells on microscopic examination. Gram stain findings consistent with bacterial vaginosis include a marked reduction or absence of Lactobacillus morphology, a predominance of Gardnerella morphotype, and few or no white blood cells. Other potential causes of vulvovaginitis, such as Trichomonas vaginalis, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Candida albicans, and herpes simplex virus, should be excluded before initiating treatment. Clindamycin vaginal ovules are contraindicated in individuals with a known hypersensitivity to clindamycin, lincomycin, or any components of the formulation. They are also contraindicated in patients with a history of regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis, or antibiotic-associated colitis. Pseudomembranous colitis, a potentially life-threatening condition, has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including clindamycin. Symptoms such as diarrhea, bloody diarrhea, or colitis may occur during or after treatment. Mild cases may resolve with drug discontinuation alone, while moderate to severe cases may require fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, and treatment with an antibacterial agent effective against Clostridium difficile. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include vulvovaginal disorders (3.4%), vaginal pain (1.9%), and vaginal yeast infections (1.5%). Less common adverse events include menstrual disorders, dysuria, pyelonephritis, vaginal discharge, abdominal cramps, fever, and localized pain. Systemic absorption of clindamycin from vaginal administration is approximately 30%, which may lead to systemic effects. Clindamycin has bacteriostatic activity and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit, similar to macrolides. It is primarily metabolized in the liver, and its pharmacokinetics following vaginal administration are not fully detailed in the drug label. In pregnant women, clindamycin vaginal ovules should be used with caution, particularly during the first trimester. Systemic administration of clindamycin during the second and third trimesters has not been associated with an increased risk of congenital abnormalities. However, abnormal labor was reported more frequently in women treated with clindamycin vaginal cream during the second trimester compared to placebo. Clindamycin is excreted in human milk following oral or parenteral administration, but it is unknown whether vaginally administered clindamycin is excreted in breast milk. Nursing mothers should weigh the potential risks to the infant against the benefits of the medication. The safety and efficacy of clindamycin vaginal ovules in pediatric patients have not been established, except for post-menarchal females, where data from adult women have been extrapolated. In geriatric patients, there is insufficient data to determine whether they respond differently from younger individuals. Clindamycin vaginal ovules are supplied in cartons containing three suppositories with one applicator. They should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with permissible temperature excursions between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F). The brand name for this medication is CLEOCIN®.
